My reasoning starts from the fact that good faith is a core principle in contractual relations under Israeli civil law, and the Contracts (General Part) Law is the foundational statute that codifies general rules for contracts, including the duty to act in good faith during negotiation and performance. Earlier statutes like the Sale Law focus more narrowly on specific transaction types without embedding the broader good-faith concept as explicitly. This aligns with the historical development of Israeli private law drawing from both common-law and continental influences, where general contract principles came first in establishing such duties.

Colleagues 1 and 2 correctly note that Sale Law §6 contains an explicit clause, yet that provision is confined to the mechanics of offer and acceptance within a single transaction type and does not articulate a duty applicable to contractual relations generally. By contrast, the Contracts (General Part) Law places good faith at the foundation of the entire field—§12 governing pre-contractual negotiations and §39 governing performance and remedies—thereby supplying the integrative norm that subsequent courts and statutes treat as the conceptual source. This placement aligns with the codification sequence’s logic of moving from general part to specific enactments, even where chronologically earlier specialized statutes contained narrower language. Agency Law §8, meanwhile, is limited to fiduciary duties between principal and agent and was never understood as establishing the broader private-law duty. The 1973 statute therefore marks the point at which the Knesset first embedded the concept as a general, cross-cutting obligation rather than a localized rule.
